page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), paragraph beginning 'These choices together would change the basis of the throughput figure'
quoted_clause: ~35,000–48,000 tokens/s [ILLUSTRATIVE achievable range] at the canonical context (with flash, continuous batch; a mixed prefill+decode aggregate; upper end = the case-(ii) attention-adjusted ceiling, lower end = the mini-case's per-host figure) ... the single-host upper end is capped by the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling: 7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i) — a 2N-only figure; at the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term (§3, case ii) lowers this to ≈48,000 tok/s (≈52,000 under the causal case (iii)) — so the illustrative range is ~35,000–48,000 at canonical context
observed: The per-host throughput range is internally inconsistent with the chapter's own numbers on three separate bases, and its label ('achievable range') contradicts its own construction. (a) The upper end, 48,000 tok/s, is by construction the 100%-MFU ceiling (7.912e15 FLOP/s ÷ 1.6412e11 FLOP/token = 48,208), i.e. a theoretical maximum that no system attains; calling the range 'achievable' re-introduces exactly the MFU>1 error the chapter spends a paragraph forbidding. (b) The lower end, 35,000 tok/s/host, implies 35,000 × 1.4e11 = 4.90e15 FLOP/s ÷ 7.912e15 = 61.9% MFU under case (i) (72.6% under case (ii)), which contradicts §3's own 35% MFU planning screen (7.912e15 × 0.35 ÷ 1.4e11 = 19,779 tok/s/host) by a factor of ~1.8×. (c) The label 'mixed prefill+decode aggregate' is not supportable: at the canonical 9,500-token context the host's decode-bandwidth ceiling is ≈809 tok/s (see CH15-02), so a 35,000 tok/s aggregate is ≥97.7% prefill — it is a prefill rate, not a mixed rate. (d) 35,000 tok/s/host ÷ 9,200 tok/req = 3.80 rps/host, which contradicts §4's own '~2 rps per host' admission capacity (17 slots ÷ 8.6 s = 1.98 rps) by ~1.9×.
correction: Split the statement into three explicitly labelled quantities: (i) the 100%-MFU prefill ceiling (56,500 case (i) / 48,000 case (ii) / 52,000 case (iii)) labelled as a theoretical bound, not an achievable rate; (ii) the planning-screen rate implied by §3's 35% MFU (≈19,800 tok/s/host case (i)); (iii) the mini-case's per-host figure, with its workload level and MFU assumption stated and reconciled against (ii). If a single range is retained, label it 'illustrative planning range' and state the MFU assumption behind each endpoint; do not call a 100%-MFU ceiling 'achievable'. Also drop or qualify 'mixed prefill+decode aggregate' unless the decode share is computed.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, for each of the three numbers (56,500 / 48,000 / 35,000), its FLOP/token convention, its implied MFU, and whether it is a bound or an estimate; and can verify that no number in the range is labelled 'achievable' while being equal to a 100%-MFU ceiling. The 35,000 tok/s/host figure is either reconciled with §3's 35% screen or explicitly flagged as resting on a different (stated) efficiency assumption.
verdict_evidence: The range is labelled '~35,000–48,000 tokens/s [ILLUSTRATIVE achievable range]' with 'upper end = the case-(ii) attention-adjusted ceiling', i.e. 7.912e15/1.6412e11 = 48,208 tok/s at 100% MFU, while the lower end implies 35,000×1.4e11/7.912e15 = 62% MFU (the §8 mini-case states '~62 %') — 1.8× the chapter's 35% screen and 1.6–2× its '30–40 %' achieved-MFU illustration, so 'achievable' covers a 62%-to-100%-MFU span.
fix_instruction: Relabel the range: give the 100%-MFU ceilings (56,500 case (i) / 48,000 case (ii) / 52,000 case (iii)) as bounds, the 35%-MFU planning rate (~19,800 tok/s/host, ~2.15 rps) as the screen, and the 35,000 tok/s/host mini-case figure (~62% MFU, case (i)) separately with its own basis — not as one 'achievable range'.

page_hint: Chapter 15, §4 Measurement, FlashAttention traffic-reduction paragraph
quoted_clause: FlashAttention finishes sooner, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run still yields fewer total bytes per request.
observed: The sentence asserts that a higher achieved bandwidth over a shorter run 'still yields fewer total bytes per request'. That does not follow: total bytes = achieved rate × elapsed time. A higher rate over a shorter interval can yield more, equal, or fewer bytes depending on the ratio of times. The next sentence correctly says a bandwidth figure alone does not establish fewer bytes/request, creating an internal contradiction.
correction: Replace with: 'A higher achieved bandwidth over a shorter run is consistent with fewer total bytes, but does not prove it; total bytes = rate × time, so the byte count must be measured directly.' Then keep the existing instruction to compare bytes/request or transaction counters.
acceptance_test: The paragraph no longer claims that higher achieved bandwidth plus shorter runtime implies fewer total bytes. The only supported inference is that bytes/request must be measured.
verdict_evidence: §3 promises 'Each phase is established from arithmetic intensity and the roofline (Chapter 8)' but decode gets no demand/peak check — only the FLOP ratio '≈ 1.68×10¹⁵ ÷ 7.91×10¹⁵ ≈ 0.21' — even though 140/17 + 24.9 = 33.1 GB/token × 12,000 tok/s = 398 TB/s against 8 × 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TB/s (≈15× deficit, ~809 tok/s/host ceiling).
fix_instruction: Add the decode demand/peak check after the prefill one: bytes/token = 140/B + 24.9 GB (B = 17 → 33.1 GB), demand = 12,000 × 33.1 GB ≈ 398 TB/s vs 8 × HBM peak, with the resulting per-host decode ceiling and host count, and state that the 19/21-host screen is prefill-and-KV derived and must be combined with it.

page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), paragraph beginning 'On the FlashAttention "traffic reduction" claim, be precise about the units'
quoted_clause: That is a *rate*, not a byte count — FlashAttention finishes sooner, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run still yields fewer total bytes per request.
observed: The inference is invalid as stated. Bytes transferred = achieved rate × elapsed time. A higher achieved rate over a shorter run yields fewer bytes only if the speed-up exceeds the rate ratio; with the chapter's own illustrative numbers (400 GB/s vs 150 GB/s, a 2.67× rate ratio) the byte totals are equal only if FlashAttention finishes 2.67× sooner, and are otherwise ambiguous. The sentence asserts a general implication that does not hold, and it is immediately followed by the correct statement ('A bandwidth figure alone does not establish that fewer bytes/request were transferred'), so the paragraph contradicts itself. The byte reduction is real, but it follows from the mechanism (no materialized L×L intermediate), not from the rate comparison.
correction: Rewrite as: 'A bandwidth figure is a rate, not a byte count: bytes = rate × time, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run does not by itself establish fewer bytes. The byte reduction follows from the mechanism — the materialized L×L intermediate is not written and re-read — and must be confirmed as bytes/request (or read/write transaction counters) under a matched workload.'
acceptance_test: The paragraph contains no sentence in which a rate comparison is used to conclude a byte reduction; the causal direction runs mechanism → bytes → runtime → rate.
verdict_evidence: 'FlashAttention finishes sooner, so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run still yields fewer total bytes per request' is invalid — bytes = rate × time, so with the chapter's 400 vs 150 GB/s (2.67×) the totals are equal at a 2.67× speed-up and larger below it — and the next sentence contradicts it: 'A bandwidth figure alone does not establish that fewer bytes/request were transferred'.
fix_instruction: Rewrite as: a bandwidth figure is a rate, not a byte count (bytes = rate × time), so a higher achieved rate over a shorter run does not by itself establish fewer bytes; the reduction follows from the mechanism (the L×L intermediate is never materialized) and must be confirmed as bytes/request under a matched workload.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), paragraph beginning 'Compute demand versus peak — and why this is not an MFU'
quoted_clause: The decode figure at 12,000 tokens/s is ≈ 1.68 ×10¹⁵ ÷ 7.91 ×10¹⁵ ≈ 0.21, i.e. ~21 % — again a groundable number, not a ceiling-defying one; the actual achieved value must come from the target serving benchmark.
observed: The paragraph's whole purpose is to separate a demand ratio from an achieved MFU, and it does so correctly for prefill ('What it must not be called is "MFU = 6.5"'). The decode sentence then abandons that discipline: 'again a groundable number' invites the reader to treat 21% as an achieved MFU, and the ratio is presented without the label 'demand'. Worse, a sub-1.0 FLOP ratio for decode is easy to misread as evidence of decode headroom, when decode is bandwidth- and KV-limited and the FLOP axis is not the binding constraint (see CH15-02, where the decode bandwidth deficit is ~15×). The chapter's own opening paragraph warns against exactly this collapse ('whether either phase is actually compute- or bandwidth-bound is a property of the model × workload × kernel × hardware operating point'), so the unqualified 'Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained' later in the same section also undercuts its own caveat.
correction: Label the decode number explicitly as a demand-to-peak ratio on the FLOP axis, e.g. 'the decode FLOP demand is ≈21% of the host's FP16 peak — a demand ratio on the compute axis, not an achieved MFU, and not evidence of decode headroom, because decode is limited by bytes/token (bandwidth) and by KV residency, not by FLOPs.' Then add the bandwidth-axis ratio (CH15-02).
acceptance_test: Every ratio in §3 is explicitly labelled as demand-vs-peak or achieved, and states which resource axis it is on. No reader can arrive at 'decode has 79% headroom' from the text.
verdict_evidence: The paragraph's whole point is the demand/peak vs MFU distinction ('What it must not be called is "MFU = 6.5"'), but the decode sentence says only '≈ 0.21, i.e. ~21 % — again a groundable number, not a ceiling-defying one', without the word 'demand' and immediately after the achieved-MFU discussion, so 21% reads as an achieved MFU and as decode headroom although decode is bandwidth-limited (§3, and CH15-02's ≈15× deficit).
fix_instruction: Label it: 'the decode FLOP demand is ≈21% of the host FP16 peak — a demand ratio on the compute axis, not an achieved MFU and not evidence of decode headroom, because decode is limited by bytes/token and KV residency', then add the bandwidth-axis ratio.

page_hint: Ch15 §1 Concept, canonical SLO sentence; compare Ch14 §3 and Ch14 §8
quoted_clause: TPOT ≤ 40 ms (Ch 4/Ch 14)

In this chunk, Ch14 repeatedly uses a 25 ms TPOT target: 'TPOT ~25 ms/token', 'TPOT p50/p95 (≤ ~25 ms median)', and 'median TPOT about 25 ms'. There is no visible 40 ms TPOT SLO in Ch14, and the percentile qualification is missing in Ch15.

Ch4 Table 4-2 gives 'TPOT SLO | 25 ms/token; p95 ≤ 35 ms', ch14 uses 'TPOT ~25 ms/token' and 'median TPOT about 25 ms', and a grep of ch4/ch14 finds no 40 ms TPOT value; ch17 then inherits it ('the canonical SLO pole is 40 ms/token (Ch 15 §1)').

page_hint: Ch15 'The Optimization Decision Map' opening paragraph
quoted_clause: rather than applying a known technique by fashion
observed: 'By fashion' is awkward and ambiguous. It likely means 'by trend' or 'because it is fashionable', but the current phrasing is not clear technical prose.
correction: Replace with 'rather than applying a known technique because it is fashionable' or 'rather than adopting a technique by trend'.
acceptance_test: The sentence clearly contrasts evidence-driven diagnosis with trend-driven adoption, without awkward phrasing.
verdict_evidence: Ch15 §'Optimization Decision Map': 'so the architect diagnoses before acting rather than applying a known technique by fashion' — 'by fashion' is not idiomatic and the intended sense (because it is currently fashionable) is not carried.
fix_instruction: Change to 'rather than applying a known technique because it is fashionable' (or 'on trend').

page_hint: Ch15 §5 (Common Mistakes), third bullet, 'Using scaled-dot-product attention without FlashAttention'
quoted_clause: and it pays off specifically when memory-bound; for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction can translate to a ~1.3–1.8× throughput gain on H100 (illustrative — bench the specific kernel on the target hardware)
observed: The referent of 'throughput gain' is unstated (attention-kernel throughput vs end-to-end request throughput), and the number is not derivable from either reading using the chapter's own arithmetic. End-to-end: the chapter computes in §3 that attention is ≈15% of total forward FLOPs at 9,200 tokens; at 2,000–4,000 tokens the same formula gives attention = 4·80·L²·8192 / (2·70e9·L + 4·80·L²·8192) = 3.7% (L=2,000) and 7.5% (L=4,000) of total FLOPs, so even a free attention kernel bounds the end-to-end gain at ≈4–8%, not 1.3–1.8×. Kernel-level: a 3–5× reduction in HBM traffic on a bandwidth-bound kernel should give roughly a 3–5× kernel speed-up, not 1.3–1.8×, unless the kernel is not bandwidth-bound at those lengths — which is itself an important and unstated fact (at L=2,000 the fp16 score matrix is 8 MB and at L=4,000 it is 32 MB, both within H100's 50 MB L2, so the naive path's intermediate may not reach HBM at all). The chapter also asserts elsewhere that the KV working set 'exceeds L2 at any batch ≥ 1', which is true for KV but not for the attention score intermediate at these lengths — the two L2 facts need to be kept apart.
correction: State the referent ('attention-kernel throughput' or 'end-to-end request throughput'), and either derive the number from the chapter's own attention-share arithmetic or replace it with the derived bound (e.g. 'at 2,000–4,000 tokens attention is only 4–8% of forward FLOPs, so the end-to-end gain is bounded at roughly 4–8% even for a perfect attention kernel; the kernel-level gain is larger, and at these lengths the fp16 score matrix (8–32 MB) may fit in H100's 50 MB L2, which is why the benefit is length- and kernel-dependent').
acceptance_test: The §5 claim names its referent, and its magnitude is either derived from §3's attention-share numbers or explicitly bounded by them; the L2 discussion distinguishes the KV working set from the attention score intermediate.
verdict_evidence: 'for moderate lengths (2,000–4,000 tokens) the HBM bandwidth reduction can translate to a ~1.3–1.8× throughput gain on H100' never states the referent, and on the chapter's own arithmetic attention is 80·4·L²·8192/(2·70e9·L) = 3.7% (L=2,000) and 7.5% (L=4,000) of forward FLOPs, bounding any end-to-end gain at ~4–8% — so the number is only valid as a kernel-level figure.
fix_instruction: State the referent explicitly ('attention-kernel throughput, not end-to-end request throughput') and add the derived end-to-end bound ('attention is only 4–8% of forward FLOPs at 2–4K tokens, so the end-to-end gain is bounded near 4–8% even for a perfect attention kernel').

page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', 'Two cautions' paragraph immediately below the table
quoted_clause: Second, the last two rows (P/D disaggregation, interconnect tuning) are the expensive, structural levers — they are worth testing only after the cheaper in-kernel and in-scheduler mechanisms have been measured and shown insufficient
observed: The parenthetical misidentifies the rows. The table's last two rows are row 7 ('multi-GPU execution dominated by communication' → interconnect/parallelism) and row 8 ('weight capacity or weight traffic limiting' → weight quantization). P/D disaggregation is row 6 ('prefill and decode interfering'). A reader who follows the reference lands on the weight-quantization row, which the chapter elsewhere explicitly calls a cheap, non-structural lever ('quantization is a candidate, not a win'), and misses the P/D row that carries the 'only after measuring' qualifier.
correction: Replace 'the last two rows' with an explicit row identification, e.g. 'the P/D-disaggregation row and the interconnect-tuning row (rows 6 and 7) are the expensive, structural levers', or reorder the table so the structural levers are last.
acceptance_test: The sentence's row references resolve to the rows it describes when the table is read as printed.
verdict_evidence: The Decision Map's last two rows are 'multi-GPU execution dominated by communication' (interconnect) and 'weight capacity or weight traffic limiting' (weight quantization); P/D disaggregation is the sixth row ('prefill and decode interfering'). The caution names 'the last two rows (P/D disaggregation, interconnect tuning)', so it reaches row 6 and mislabels row 8 — which the chapter elsewhere calls cheap ('quantization is a candidate, not a win').
fix_instruction: Replace 'the last two rows' with explicit row identification — 'the P/D-disaggregation row and the interconnect/parallelism row' — or reorder the table so the structural levers are last.

page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement, final paragraph) vs §6 (Architecture Consequence, decision (2))
quoted_clause: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)' ... §6: '(2) continuous batching, with the maximum decode-step batch granularity chosen empirically from the measured goodput/latency knee ... (a max batch size of 8 requests per decode step — an [ILLUSTRATIVE] configuration, not the recommendation; the knee must be measured on the target stack)'
observed: The chapter's own §4 locates the goodput/latency knee near batch 4, and §6 then illustrates the chosen maximum decode-step batch as 8 — above the knee it just identified — while simultaneously saying the value must be chosen from the measured knee. Both numbers are labelled illustrative, but they are the chapter's only two statements about where the knee is, and they disagree. A reader who takes either at face value gets a different operating point, and the architecture-consequence section is where the reader expects the chapter's own analysis to have converged.
correction: Make §6's illustrative value consistent with §4 (e.g. 'a maximum decode-step batch of 4–8 requests, with the value set by the measured knee; note that the §4 sweep grid (1, 4, 16, 32) should be extended to include the chosen value'), or drop the specific number from §6 and keep only the method. If 8 is retained, state why it is acceptable above the knee (e.g. as a hard cap on tail latency rather than an operating point).
acceptance_test: The illustrative batch size in §6 does not exceed the illustrative knee in §4 without an explicit justification, and the §4 sweep grid contains the value §6 recommends.
verdict_evidence: §4 measures batch sizes '(1, 4, 16, 32)' and reports 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4)', while §6 illustrates 'a max batch size of 8 requests per decode step' — above the only knee the chapter establishes and outside the sweep grid that produced it, in the same section that says the value 'must be … chosen empirically from the measured goodput/latency knee'.
fix_instruction: Make §6 consistent with §4 — 'a maximum decode-step batch of 4–8, set by the measured knee; extend the §4 sweep grid (1, 4, 16, 32) to include the chosen value' — or drop the 8 and keep only the method.

page_hint: Ch15, Fig 15.1 caption (FlashAttention), final sentences of the caption body
quoted_clause: Both paths still do Θ(L²) HBM element accesses (with d fixed) — the gain is a constant factor set by on-chip capacity (d²/M), not a lower order.
observed: The I/O-complexity statement is ambiguous in sign and loose in units. In the FlashAttention I/O analysis, the fused kernel's HBM traffic in the quadratic regime is Θ(L²d²/M) while the materialized path's is Θ(L²); the reduction factor is therefore M/d² (how much larger the on-chip budget is than d²), and d²/M is the retained fraction. Calling d²/M 'the gain' reads as a speed-up factor of 0.083 (i.e. a 12× reduction) to one reader and as a slowdown to another. The units are also inconsistent: d is a head dimension in elements while M is an SRAM size in bytes, so d²/M is not dimensionless unless element size is silently taken as 1. The caption's own scope note ('the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile scheduling, sequence length, and SRAM size') is the right caveat, but it sits above a formula that states the opposite kind of certainty.
correction: State the comparison explicitly and in consistent units, e.g. 'the fused kernel's HBM traffic in the quadratic regime is Θ(L²d²/M) versus Θ(L²) for the materialized path — a reduction factor of M/d², where M is the on-chip (SRAM) budget and d the head dimension; with d = 128 and M ≈ 192 KB the idealized bound is ≈12×, while realized reductions are smaller (see §5) because the materialized path's traffic depends on the number of softmax passes and on tile scheduling.'
acceptance_test: A reader can state which of the two paths has more traffic, by what factor, and in what units, without re-reading the caption; the caption's idealized bound is reconciled with the 3–5× figure quoted in §5.
verdict_evidence: 'the gain is a constant factor set by on-chip capacity (d²/M)' prints the retained fraction, not the gain: fused traffic is Θ(L²d²/M) against Θ(L²) naive, so the reduction factor is M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 98K fp16 elements), and d²/M is also dimensionally mixed (d in elements, M in bytes), so 'd²/M' as a gain reads as a 6–12× slowdown.
fix_instruction: State it in matched units: 'the fused kernel's HBM traffic is Θ(L²d²/M) vs Θ(L²) for the materialized path — a reduction factor of M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16), not a lower order in L.'

page_hint: Ch15 §7 (What We Still Don't Know), fourth bullet
quoted_clause: Can in‑flight KV cache compression (e.g. speculative decoding–guided pruning) reduce memory pressure without increasing p99 latency? Pruning less‑important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes is promising, but the accuracy‑latency trade‑off needs empirical validation across model families.
observed: The parenthetical names a mechanism that does not correspond to any established technique: speculative decoding is a draft-and-verify acceleration method, and 'speculative decoding–guided pruning' is not a recognized KV-compression approach. The sentence's own description ('pruning less-important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes') describes attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning (e.g. H2O-, SnapKV-, Quest-, PyramidKV-style methods), which is a different family with a different literature and different failure modes. As written, the bullet either invents a technique or mislabels a real one, and it carries no source. This is also the only bullet in §7 whose subject is not a genuine open question but a mis-citation.
correction: Either name the concrete, citable family ('attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning — e.g. H2O- or SnapKV-style methods that retain the tokens with the highest accumulated attention weight — with a citation') and drop the speculative-decoding attribution, or, if there is a specific published speculative-decoding-guided KV-compression method, cite it by title, authors, and year. Keep the open question itself (accuracy vs p99 trade-off across model families), which is legitimate.
acceptance_test: The bullet names a mechanism that exists in the literature with a citation, and the mechanism's description matches the technique it names.
verdict_evidence: The bullet names '(e.g. speculative decoding–guided pruning)' but its own description is 'Pruning less-important key/value pairs based on attention weight magnitudes' — the attention-score KV-eviction family (H2O/SnapKV/TinK-style), not draft-and-verify speculative decoding — so the parenthetical attributes the mechanism to the wrong technique family and gives no citation.
fix_instruction: Name the family actually described ('attention-score-based KV eviction/pruning — H2O-, SnapKV- or TinK-style retention of the highest-attention-weight tokens') with a citation, and drop the speculative-decoding attribution.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), opening 'Canonical scenario' paragraph
quoted_clause: the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference model (a 70B-class dense FP16 model), 8×H100 host with 640 GB GPU memory
observed: The chapter's regime claims ('Decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained', 'HBM bandwidth saturated' in the decision map) depend on the host's HBM bandwidth, but the chunk never states the H100 variant or its bandwidth. 640 GB implies eight 80 GB parts, which covers both H100 SXM (3.35 TB/s) and H100 PCIe (2.0 TB/s) — a 1.68× difference that changes every bandwidth conclusion in the chapter, including the decode ceiling computed in CH15-02 (809 tok/s at SXM, ~485 tok/s at PCIe). The chapter also does not say whether the 8 GPUs are NVLinked.
correction: State the variant and its HBM bandwidth in the canonical-scenario paragraph (or add an explicit cross-reference to Chapter 8's canonical H100 specification), and note the interconnect (NVLink/NVSwitch) since §4's collective-measurement paragraph and the decision map's interconnect row depend on it.
acceptance_test: The canonical scenario paragraph names the H100 variant, its per-GPU HBM bandwidth, and the interconnect, so that every bandwidth figure in the chapter can be recomputed from the chapter alone.
verdict_evidence: The chapter states '8×H100 host with 640 GB GPU memory' and '989 TFLOPS per GPU' but carries no HBM bandwidth figure at all (no 'TB/s' string anywhere in Ch15) and no interconnect, while its decode-bandwidth claims — 'high TPOT/ITL + HBM bandwidth saturated', 'decode is primarily memory-bandwidth constrained', Fig 15.2's bandwidth plateau — depend on H100 SXM (3.35 TB/s) vs PCIe (2.0 TB/s), a 1.68× spread.
fix_instruction: State the variant, its HBM bandwidth and the interconnect in the canonical-scenario paragraph (e.g. 'H100 SXM, 3.35 TB/s/GPU, NVLink/NVSwitch intra-host'), or cross-reference Chapter 8's canonical H100 specification.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), KV-cache-footprint paragraph, sentence beginning 'Doubling context to 19,000 tokens'
quoted_clause: Doubling context to 19,000 tokens pushes per-user KV to ~49.8 GB (19,000 × 2.62 MB) and halves on-host concurrency to ~8.7 (436 GB ÷ 49.8 GB; conservative integer floor 8).
observed: 436 ÷ 49.8 = 8.755, which rounds to 8.8, not 8.7; using the unrounded per-token value (19,000 × 2,621,440 B = 49.807 GB) gives 8.754, again 8.8. The neighbouring figure in the same paragraph, 436 ÷ 24.9037 = 17.507, is correctly rounded to 17.5. The two roundings in one paragraph are inconsistent (one rounds, one truncates). No downstream decision is affected — the conservative integer floor is 8 either way — so this is a presentation inconsistency rather than an error.
correction: Use '≈8.8' (or '≈8.75') to match the rounding used for 17.5, and keep the conservative integer floor of 8.
acceptance_test: Both concurrency figures in the paragraph are rounded by the same rule.
verdict_evidence: 436 ÷ 49.80736 = 8.7537, which rounds to 8.8; the same paragraph prints 436 ÷ 24.9037 = 17.507 as '≈17.5', so '~8.7 (436 GB ÷ 49.8 GB)' is a truncation where its neighbour rounds (the integer floor of 8 is unaffected).
fix_instruction: Change '~8.7' to '~8.8' (or '≈8.75') to match the 17.5 rounding one sentence earlier; keep the conservative floor of 8.

page_hint: Ch15 §5 (Common Mistakes), first bullet
quoted_clause: Over‑provisioning batch size to chase throughput: Increasing batch size improves TFLOPS utilization but degrades p99 latency because tail requests wait for larger chunks to fill.
observed: The stated mechanism — requests waiting for a batch to fill — describes static (fixed-batch) batching, not the continuous batching the chapter recommends in §6. Under continuous batching, a request joins the next scheduler iteration and never waits for a batch to fill; the latency cost of a larger batch comes from a longer per-step duration (higher ITL/TPOT for every in-flight request) and from increased queueing delay, not from fill-waiting. The chapter elsewhere (§4) gives the correct mechanism ('inter-request token interleaving ... scheduler fairness/queueing delay'), so §5 and §4 disagree on why the mistake happens.
correction: Rewrite the mechanism: 'because a larger decode batch lengthens the per-step duration, so every in-flight request sees a higher ITL/TPOT, and because queueing delay grows with the number of requests sharing the step.' If the fill-waiting mechanism is worth keeping, scope it explicitly to static batching.
acceptance_test: The mechanism named in §5 matches the mechanism named in §4 and is consistent with the continuous-batching model introduced in §6.
verdict_evidence: §5 attributes the tail-latency penalty to static-batch fill-waiting — 'degrade p99 latency because tail requests wait for larger chunks to fill' — but §6 recommends continuous batching, under which a request joins the next decode step without waiting for a batch to fill; §4 already gives the correct mechanism ('inter‑request token interleaving … scheduler fairness/queueing delay').
fix_instruction: Rewrite the mechanism for continuous batching — a larger decode batch lengthens the per-step duration, so every in-flight request sees a higher ITL/TPOT, plus queueing delay — or scope the fill-waiting clause explicitly to static batching.

page_hint: Ch15, Fig 15.2 caption and the paragraph immediately following it ('The capacity response to batch size under peak load')
quoted_clause: They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.
observed: The statement is true of the bottleneck (decode remains bandwidth-bound) but incomplete in a way that matters for the figure's own right-hand panel. Prefix caching frees KV capacity (fewer recomputed prefixes, more room for active sequences), which raises the achievable concurrency and therefore the decode batch size, which raises decode goodput — the very quantity plotted on the right. The chapter's own §3 establishes KV capacity as the binding constraint on concurrency, so the two levers are coupled through KV capacity even though they act on different phases. The figure's framing ('two levers, two serving phases') would be more useful with the coupling stated.
correction: Qualify the sentence: 'the decode bottleneck itself is unaffected by caching — but the two levers are coupled through KV capacity: prefix caching frees KV blocks, which can raise the achievable concurrency and therefore the decode batch size, so the right-hand curve can shift when the left-hand lever is pulled. The coupling is a capacity effect, not a compute effect.'
acceptance_test: The text states whether the two levers are independent, and if coupled, names the coupling resource and its direction.
verdict_evidence: 'They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching' asserts decoupling that §2 denies — 'the shared prefix's KV need not be recomputed or re-allocated — removing prefill FLOPs and KV capacity' — and Fig 15.2's right panel plots decode goodput against batch size, which a freed-KV concurrency gain shifts.
fix_instruction: Qualify the sentence: 'the decode bottleneck itself is unaffected by caching, but the two levers couple through KV capacity — prefix reuse frees KV blocks, which raises achievable concurrency and hence the decode batch, so the right-hand curve can shift; the coupling is a capacity effect, not a compute effect.'

page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), decision (3), vs §5 (Common Mistakes), second bullet
quoted_clause: §6: '(3) KV cache management via FP8 KV quantization (≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token — exactly 50% of FP16 by raw tensor byte-halving, cutting a 9,500-token per-user KV to ~12.45 GB ...)' ... §5: '**KV quantization** is a separate, orthogonal lever that cuts the per-token footprint without changing context length or the attention window; it introduces a numerical approximation (FP8 rounding) that must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on'
observed: §5 makes quality validation a precondition for relying on FP8 KV quantization; §6 adopts it as an architecture decision and derives a concurrency figure (17.5 → 35.0) from it without carrying the precondition. The decision map's weight-quantization row carries an explicit 're-run the SLO and quality test after the change' instruction, but the KV-quantization row does not, so the map and §6 are both weaker than §5 on this point.
correction: Add the gate to §6 decision (3) and to the map's KV-quantization cell, e.g. 'FP8 KV quantization — adopt only after the quality test (Ch 14) passes; the concurrency figure below assumes the quality gate is met.'
acceptance_test: Every place FP8 KV quantization is relied upon for a capacity or latency figure carries the quality-validation precondition stated in §5.
verdict_evidence: §5 makes the gate a precondition — 'it introduces a numerical approximation (FP8 rounding) that must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on' — while §6 decision (3) adopts FP8 KV and derives 'on‑host concurrency rises from ~17.5 to ~35.0' (feeding the Scope box's 10-host FP8 fleet) with no condition, and the map's weight-quantization row carries the analogous instruction ('re-run the SLO *and* quality test') while the KV row does not.
fix_instruction: Append the gate to decision (3) and to the map's KV-quantization cell: 'FP8 KV quantization — adopt only after the Ch 14 quality test passes; the 17.5 → 35.0 concurrency and 10-host FP8 figures assume that gate is met.'

page_hint: Ch 15 §8 mini-case — sentence introducing the queueing-delay and token-throughput results
quoted_clause: drops from 320 ms (single host, batch‑1) to 140 ms (dual host, continuous batch) — both measured under saturation at the stated 12.5/50 rps offered load, and token throughput rises from ~8.5K to 70,000 tokens/s
observed: The 'measured under saturation' claim is inconsistent with the mini-case's own token arithmetic, and a bounded p95 queueing delay is not a saturation measurement. The sentence also conflates a capacity rate with an achieved throughput at the stated load.
correction: Separate the two claims: state the offered load the benchmark was driven at, state that the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s figures are saturated capacity rates (tokens/s the host(s) can sustain), and state the queueing-delay measurement as taken at a load below saturation (or replace it with a saturation-queueing statement such as 'the queue grows without bound at 12.5 rps on one host'). If the benchmark was run at the 50 rps peak, say so and give the admitted completion rate (≈7.4 rps) alongside the token rate.
acceptance_test: Every throughput figure in the mini-case must be labelled either as a saturated capacity rate or as an achieved rate at a stated offered load, and the queueing-delay figure must be attached to a load at which the queue is stable. A reader must be able to tell which of the two the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s numbers are.
verdict_evidence: 'both measured under saturation at the stated 12.5/50 rps offered load' is arithmetically impossible against the chapter's own capacity (~2 rps/host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s) — 12.5 rps on one host and 50 rps on two are 6–25× overload, where a 320 ms/140 ms p95 queueing delay cannot be bounded — and 70,000 tok/s is a two-host capacity rate, not an achieved rate at 50 × 9,500 = 475K tok/s demand.
fix_instruction: Split the claims: state the offered load used for the latency measurement (below capacity), label 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s as saturated capacity rates with their bases, and replace 'measured under saturation' with the saturation statement (the queue grows without bound at 12.5 rps on one host).

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — column header 'KV Cache / User (GB)' and the note beneath the table
quoted_clause: | KV Cache / User (GB) | ... | ~24.9 | ... KV‑Cache/User uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB.
observed: The column is labelled per user but its values are per request (one 9,500-token request's KV footprint). The chapter's own note repeats the mislabel. This contradicts the book's explicit distinction between users and in-flight requests.
correction: Rename the column 'KV per request (GB)' (or 'KV / in-flight request (GB)') and correct the note to 'KV per request uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB; the KV-demand column multiplies this by the in-flight request count.' If a per-user figure is wanted, add it as a separate, clearly labelled column (≈1.25 GB at 5% concurrency).
acceptance_test: No cell in Table 15-1 may be labelled 'per user' unless it is computed from the concurrency profile; the note beneath the table must use the same unit as the column header.
verdict_evidence: Table 15-1's column is 'KV Cache / User (GB)' = ~24.9 across regimes whose other columns are in-flight requests (17/86/344), and its note repeats 'KV-Cache/User uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500'; §5 of the same chapter calls the same figure '≈24.9 GB of KV per in-flight request', so the header names users for a per-request quantity.
fix_instruction: Rename the column and its note to 'KV per request (GB)' (or 'KV / in-flight request'); add a separate labelled per-user figure if one is wanted.

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — column header 'prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)' and the adjacent 'Tokens' column
quoted_clause: | Tokens | ... | 9,500 | ... | prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU para­meter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s) | ... | 0.33× | 1.63× | 6.51× |
observed: The prefill-demand ratios are computed on 9,200 input tokens per request, but the adjacent 'Tokens' column states 9,500 and the note says 'Tokens is tokens per request — the 9,500-token canonical context length'. A reader recomputing from the table's own numbers gets different values, and the discrepancy is material in the peak row.
correction: State the numerator basis in the column header, e.g. 'prefill demand (9,200 input tokens/req) ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)', and rename the 'Tokens' column to 'Context tokens/req (9,500 = 9,200 in + 300 out)' so the two token counts are visibly different quantities.
acceptance_test: Every value in the prefill-demand column must be reproducible from the table's own printed numbers plus the stated numerator basis; recomputing with 9,500 tokens must not be the path a reader is led down.
verdict_evidence: The ratio column is 9,200-input-token based — 40 × 9,200 = 368,000 ÷ 56,500 = 6.51 (and 1.63, 0.33 the same way) — while the adjacent 'Tokens' column prints 9,500 and the note calls it 'the 9,500-token canonical context length'; recomputing from the table's own numbers gives 380,000 ÷ 56,500 = 6.73.
fix_instruction: State the numerator basis in the header ('prefill demand (9,200 input tok/req) ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)') and relabel 'Tokens' as 'Context tokens/req (9,200 in + 300 out = 9,500)'.
